findings.title: verify() never expires sessions
findings.description: verify() returns the session whenever the token matches, without checking expires_at, despite the contract that an expired token is unknown. Sessions therefore live forever.

findings.title: require_admin() always rejects everyone
findings.description: The condition `role != "admin" || role != "owner"` is true for every possible role, so no session can ever pass the admin check.

findings.title: bearer_token() can overflow and dereference null
findings.description: A fixed 64-byte stack buffer is filled with strcpy(header), allowing overflow on long headers, and `space + 1` is dereferenced even when no space exists, causing a crash on malformed/empty Authorization headers.

findings.title: Cache destructor leaks Entry objects
findings.description: entries_ holds raw Entry* allocated with new; clear() only drops the pointers, leaking every cached entry on destruction.

findings.title: Expired entry erased from map but leaked
findings.description: get() calls entries_.erase(it) after finding an expired entry, leaking the Entry* allocated for it.

findings.title: set() leaks entries and evicts by map key, not LRU
findings.description: On overflow set() erases an iterator without deleting it, and if a code already exists the old Entry* is overwritten without deletion. Eviction also picks entries_.begin() (key order) instead of the least recently used entry, contradicting the documented behavior.

findings.title: erase() leaks the Entry*
findings.description: entries_.erase(code) discards the stored pointer without deleting it.

findings.title: sweep() invalidates its iterator while erasing
findings.description: Calling entries_.erase(it) inside a range-for then incrementing `it` is undefined behavior and can skip or corrupt entries, so expired cache entries are not reliably removed.

findings.title: utilization() underflows due to integer division order
findings.description: size / limit * 100 evaluates to 0 for any partially full cache, and divides by zero when limit_ is 0.

findings.title: resolve() deletes valid links and keeps expired ones
findings.description: The expiry check is inverted: it erases the link and returns false when `now < expires_at` (still valid), and resolves expired links as if usable. Every successful lookup therefore destroys the link.

findings.title: rename() validates `from` twice instead of `to`
findings.description: validate_code(from) is called twice, so an invalid destination code is never rejected before use.

findings.title: page() overruns the vector by one
findings.description: When offset+size exceeds the size, end is set to all.size()+1, so the returned slice reads one past the end.

findings.title: success_rate() truncates to zero
findings.description: `used / links_.size() * 100` performs integer division first, yielding 0 unless every link has hits.

findings.title: remove() never decrements the owner quota
findings.description: The quota counter is incremented on create but not decremented on remove, so deleted links keep consuming the owner's quota slot.

findings.title: top() returns the least-followed links
findings.description: Sorting with a.hits < b.hits orders ascending, but the leaderboard contract calls for most hits first.

findings.title: by_owner() matches owners by substring
findings.description: owner.find(owner) != npos returns links for any owner whose name contains the query, rather than an exact match.

findings.title: extend() revives expired links
findings.description: expiry is unconditionally reset to now+ttl even when the link is already expired, contradicting the rule that an expired code must never come back to life.

findings.title: import_all() is not atomic
findings.description: Validation and insertion are interleaved, so a later invalid code leaves earlier links stored; the contract requires all-or-nothing.

findings.title: prune() returns size instead of removed count and mis-iterates
findings.description: links_.erase(it) inside the loop invalidates the iterator and removed++ logic then `++it` is undefined behavior; the function also returns links_.size() instead of the number removed.

findings.title: last_code() returns the lexically last code, not the most recent
findings.description: It assigns newest on every map iteration, so it returns the largest key by sort order rather than the most recently created link.

findings.title: Milliseconds parsed as seconds for timeout
findings.description: LINKD_TIMEOUT_MS is documented as milliseconds, but Seconds{ms} treats the value as seconds, making timeouts ~1000x too long.

findings.title: Milliseconds parsed as seconds for cache TTL
findings.description: LINKD_CACHE_TTL_MS is documented as milliseconds, but Seconds{atoi(ttl)} treats it as seconds.

findings.title: LINKD_FETCH_LIMIT is parsed then discarded
findings.description: parsed is `(void)`-ed and never assigned to cfg.fetch_limit, so the environment override has no effect.

findings.title: validate() always returns true
findings.description: Even when problems are collected and printed, the function returns true, so invalid configurations pass startup validation.

findings.title: format_row() returns a dangling pointer
findings.description: row is a local stack buffer, so the returned const char* points to freed storage and reads are undefined behavior.

findings.title: Janitor loop erases while iterating the store map
findings.description: store.all().erase(it) inside the for loop invalidates the iterator, causing undefined behavior while sweeping expired links.

findings.title: stop_janitor() never joins the thread
findings.description: g_janitor is never joined or deleted, leaking the thread and racing with process exit after g_running is cleared.

findings.title: warm_cache() never joins worker threads
findings.description: The function returns with std::thread objects still joinable; their destructors then call std::terminate, crashing the process.

findings.title: check_targets() reads one past the vector end
findings.description: The loop condition is `i <= links.size()`, so the final iteration accesses links[links.size()], out of bounds.

findings.title: stats() divides by zero on an empty store
findings.description: g_store->total_hits() / g_store->size() is undefined behavior when no links exist.

findings.title: Startup ignores validate() result
findings.description: validate(g_cfg) is called but its return value is discarded, so the service starts even with an invalid configuration.

findings.title: TTL hour multiplication can overflow
findings.description: std::atoi(...) * 3600 is computed in int and can overflow for large ttl inputs before being converted to Seconds.

findings.title: Metrics::errors_ is uninitialized
findings.description: errors_ has no initializer, so errors() returns indeterminate garbage and the /stats response reads uninitialized memory.

findings.title: warm_cache spawns threads that are never joined
findings.description: warm_cache pushes std::thread objects into a local vector and returns without joining them. Each thread destructor runs while the thread is still joinable, which calls std::terminate and crashes the process. Additionally, every worker captures the loop variable `link` by reference, so even if joined the closures would race on the single evolving reference and read freed/changed state. Scenario: any caller of warm_cache with a non-empty link list aborts the whole service.

findings.title: Janitor thread is never joined and outlives the objects it touches
findings.description: start_janitor allocates a std::thread and keeps only an unmanaged pointer; stop_janitor only flips the atomic flag and never joins. The thread can still be sleeping or iterating store/cache when the Store/Cache are destroyed or stop_janitor returns, so it reads freed memory and leaks the thread. Scenario: process shutdown or a restart calls stop_janitor and then destructs globals, racing with the janitor loop.

findings.title: Cache shared state is accessed without synchronization
findings.description: Cache::get/set/erase/sweep/peek mutate or read `entries_` and `hits_` with no mutex or atomics. The janitor calls sweep() every interval while request paths call get/set, so two threads can erase/find/insert the same map concurrently and corrupt it or free a dangling Entry*. hits_ is a plain long incremented without atomicity. Scenario: one request in get() while the janitor sweeps expired entries -> allocator corruption or use-after-free on Entry*.

findings.title: verify() returns an interior pointer into an unprotected map
findings.description: sessions_ is a std::map with no synchronization, and verify() returns `&pair.second`, a pointer that becomes dangling when issue()/revoke() insert or erase entries (map node freed). Concurrent request threads can therefore dereference stale pointers. Scenario: thread A verifies token X while thread B revokes X -> thread A follows a freed Session, crashing or reading attacker-influenced memory.

findings.title: Metrics counters are non-atomic shared mutable state
findings.description: add_resolved/add_created increment plain long members with no synchronization while request threads call them concurrently, which is a data race and lost updates. errors_ is additionally never initialized in the declared default, so reading errors() yields an indeterminate value (undefined behavior) even single-threaded. Scenario: two concurrent requests increment resolved_ and one update is lost, skewing the dashboard; errors() reports garbage.

findings.title: Store exposes and mutates its map without synchronization
findings.description: Store uses a plain std::map with no mutex; create/resolve/rename/remove/prune/count_for_owner and the janitor (which calls store.all() and erases directly) all touch links_ and quota_ concurrently. all() hands out a direct reference to the internal map, letting callers mutate it without any coordination. Scenario: janitor pruning expired links while a redirect resolves the same code -> iterator invalidation and use-after-free.

findings.title: Stack buffer overflow in bearer_token
findings.description: bearer_token copies the unbounded Authorization header into a fixed 64-byte stack buffer with std::strcpy. An attacker can send a long header and overflow the stack, enabling control-flow hijacking. It also dereferences space+1 even when no space exists.

findings.title: Path traversal via export name
findings.description: export_csv and read_report build file paths by concatenating the user-supplied name without sanitization or confinement checks, so a name like ../../etc/passwd allows writing and reading arbitrary files under the service account.

findings.title: Path traversal via owner filename in archive_all
findings.description: archive_all writes one file per owner using pair.first directly in the path, so a crafted owner value containing path separators or .. can write outside the export directory.

findings.title: Admin authorization trusts spoofable X-Admin header
findings.description: admin_quotas grants admin access based solely on the client-supplied X-Admin header without tying it to the authenticated session or role, so any logged-in user can read admin quota data by adding the header.

findings.title: delete_link enforces no ownership check
findings.description: Although documented as owner-only, delete_link removes any code without consulting the authenticated session, letting any user delete any other user's links.

findings.title: Open redirect in /out endpoint
findings.description: The out handler redirects to the unvalidated next query parameter, allowing attackers to craft links that bounce users to arbitrary sites (phishing) while appearing to originate from this service.

findings.title: Predictable session tokens
findings.description: issue mints tokens from std::rand(), which is deterministic unless seeded and trivially predictable, allowing session fixation/hijacking. Tokens are also logged to stdout.

findings.title: Hardcoded fallback secret
findings.description: When LINKD_SECRET is unset, the authenticator silently uses a known default secret, letting anyone forge tokens or HMACs in dev or misconfigured deployments.

findings.title: Expired sessions never invalidated
findings.description: verify returns a session based only on token equality and never checks expires_at, so issued tokens remain valid indefinitely despite the 12-hour lifetime.

findings.title: Weak password hashing
findings.description: hash_password uses a trivial djb2-style hash with no salt and 64 bits of state, which is fast to brute force and vulnerable to collisions. It is unsuitable for password storage.

findings.title: secret_equals leaks via timing and early return
findings.description: secret_equals returns early on length mismatch and on the first differing byte and prints/logically differs, allowing an attacker to recover the expected value byte by byte through timing.

findings.title: Permissive CORS with credentials
findings.description: The server sends Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * together with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true, which permits cross-origin credential-bearing requests and increases CSRF risk.

findings.title: Token echoed in 401 response
findings.description: The unauthorized response includes the presented token, leaking tokens to logs/proxies and aiding token theft or fixation.

findings.title: Fixed world-writable temp path for snapshots
findings.description: write_snapshot always writes to /tmp/linkd-snapshot.json and then renames it, exposing a TOCTOU race and allowing symlink-based overwrite of attacker-chosen files.
